opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think what's really striking to me is that even with all the limitations — the low resolution, the fact that it only runs at around one frame per second, the consistency issues over longer horizons — the model learned something genuinely meaningful about interactivity without ever being told what an action is. We trained it purely on unlabeled internet videos, mostly 2D platformer gameplay, and it discovered a latent action space on its own. So when you prompt it with an image, even something it's never seen before, like a child's sketch or a photo of a real-world scene, you can actually step through it and the character responds in a fairly consistent way. Pressing the same latent action tends to produce the same kind of movement, like jumping or moving left.

That, to me, is the exciting part. It's not that the environments are polished games yet — they're clearly not. It's that we have evidence you can learn controllable world models from the vast amount of video that exists out there, without needing action labels. Action-labeled data is really scarce and expensive, whereas video is basically abundant.

And there are some fun emergent behaviors too. We saw things like parallax, where foreground and background layers move at different speeds, which the model just picked up from the data. We also saw signs of it understanding deformable objects and physics to some degree.

Longer term, what excites me is the idea of using these generated worlds as a kind of endless curriculum for training agents. If you can generate a near-infinite variety of environments, you could train more general agents that aren't overfit to a handful of hand-designed simulators. We did some early experiments on the robotics side too, showing the same approach could learn actions from robot videos. So the limitations are real, but the direction feels really promising.

r001.rationale: The response says you can prompt Genie with an image, step through the environment, and see the character respond consistently, identifying that interactivity as exciting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that excites me most is actually less about the fidelity of any single environment and more about what it means that you can get one at all from just an image. Traditionally, if you wanted an agent to learn in an interactive world, somebody had to sit down and build that world. You had to write the simulator, define the physics, define the action space, all of that. And that's a huge bottleneck, both in terms of effort and in terms of diversity. You end up with a handful of environments that everybody trains on, and agents that are very good at exactly those.

With Genie, the model learned the notion of controllability purely from watching videos. Nobody labeled the actions. It discovered on its own that there's something like "move left" or "jump" that's consistent across all of these different games and scenes, and then it lets you apply that to a frame it's never seen before. You can take a sketch, or a photo, or a generated image, and suddenly it's a place you can act in. To me that's the really interesting part, because it means the space of possible environments is basically as big as the space of images.

And yes, the limitations are very real. The environments are short, they drift, the memory is limited, things can be inconsistent if you walk away and come back. It's not a replacement for a real simulator today. But I think about it less as "is this a good game" and more as "is this a good source of experience." Even an imperfect environment can be useful for an agent if it captures the right structure, like what happens when I take this action in this kind of scene. And because the latent actions are shared, you can also run the model in reverse, in a sense, and infer what actions were taken in real videos, which opens up this huge pool of unlabeled data for training agents. So the imperfections are the current state of the technology, but the direction, where interactive worlds become something you generate rather than something you handcraft, is what I find really compelling.

astra-6.text: What I find interesting is that you can take an image and turn it into something you can interact with. It may not be a perfectly consistent world, but your actions influence what happens next. That opens up an interesting possibility for training agents: could we generate environments where they can practice, rather than having to build every environment by hand? The big question is whether those environments have enough consistency for an agent to learn something useful, and whether what it learns transfers beyond that generated world.
